parent_turns: My three-year-old is restless while I fold laundry. Give us one little pretend game we can start right here. No props, no counting, and I cannot read a long explanation.
My three-year-old and seven-year-old both want to play with our six big blocks. Give them one cooperative building game where both have a real job. No winner, no extra materials, and no writing.
We have two minutes before leaving and no materials handy. Give me one silly game to say aloud and play with my five-year-old. Two short sentences, please.

Make two big picture choices for my three-year-old: stretch tall like a giraffe or curl small like a hedgehog. We only have my phone, no printer. Show the body positions clearly so we can copy one. No worksheet boxes.

Show my five-year-old how to make a little paper tunnel from one sheet with one fold. We have no scissors or tape. Use big before-and-after pictures showing which way the paper stands, with very short instructions.
Give us one playful thing to build with one sheet of paper. We have no scissors or tape.
That is too tricky for us. Give us a much simpler build that works with the same sheet, and tell me exactly how to start.
We only have two large plastic cups. Give my five-year-old one tiny building challenge and one thing to change after trying it. No extra supplies or scorekeeping.
Make a big picture-choice page with a snail, a butterfly and a ladybug. My five-year-old will point to the one with a shell, the one with big wings, and the one with spots. No writing.
Keep these exact pictures, remove any answer boxes, and make the pictures bigger.
Keep that layout. Replace only the snail with a turtle, still showing a shell. Keep the butterfly and ladybug pictures exactly the same.
We have been looking at triangles and squares. Just keeping you in the loop.
Could you give us a few different ways to explore those together?
Why is that still a square when we turn it onto a corner? And can we try something without drawing?
My five-year-old is curious about shadows. What changes if we move a toy closer to our flashlight, and why?
Can you show that with pictures so she can compare the two positions?
What if we move the light instead and leave the toy still?
We noticed some fallen leaves float in a bowl and some sink. Just saving that observation.
What might make them behave differently, and what are a couple of ways we could check?
Could we do the second idea without tearing the leaves?
Why does a magnet stick to our fridge?
Now something different: give us one tiny pretend game about space with no props.
How could we play that sitting down, and what can my three-year-old do while the older one leads?
